notes: Correct exact comparison used consistently in Eq, compareGet and where with good tests, but it leaves the now-dead else-if float branch in where, duplicates the operator list, and places CompareNumbers in convert.go.

Exact comparison is correct and used consistently in `Eq`, `compareGet` and `Where` via an early-return `numericOpMatches` helper, but the operator list is duplicated and the now-mostly-dead `ToFloat64E` mixed-number branch is left in `where.go`.

Adds an exact CompareNumbers that handles NaN, the 2^63/2^64 bounds and fractional parts; it is wired into Eq, compareGet and where, and the old numeric code in where is cleanly removed, though returning (float64(c), 0) from compareGet is a little hacky.

Correct exact `CompareNumbers` with an inline numeric fast path in `Where` that also cleanly removes the now-unused `fmvp` float comparisons; `Eq` and `compareGet` are consistent, and the integration test covers both the compare funcs and `where`.

CompareNumbers is correct (compareFloat is somewhat convoluted), and the Eq and compareGet integration is minimal and clean, but where.go keeps the old int/uint/float relational code, now dead and including the overflow-prone int64(v.Uint()) path.

Correct exact comparison in a new `hreflect/compare.go` with a thorough unit test, but `compareFloat`'s combined `isInt` switch is harder to read, and `where.go` keeps the old int/uint/float64 branches and the `ToFloat64E` path as leftover code behind the new early return.

Closely mirrors the reference by feeding the CompareNumbers result into the existing where int64 path, with explicit NaN handling so ne returns true, and backs it with very thorough tests including a six-way eq/ne/lt/le/gt/ge consistency check.

Adds an exact `CompareNumbers` (int/uint/float, ±Inf, 2^63/2^64 boundaries, NaN) and wires it into `Eq`, `compareGet` and `Where`, mirroring the reference's 'feed c into the int64 path' approach, with NaN mapped to float NaN for IEEE semantics; it has the most extensive unit, consistency and integration tests.

Closest in spirit to the reference: internal names always get an explicit internal-issuer policy, site-block policies win, and names are forced into the automate loader regardless of auto_https; but it duplicates the public/internal split logic inline, skips the global renewal_window_ratio, and can emit empty public policies.

Focused inline implementation that, unlike the others, explicitly assigns the internal issuer even when every listed name is internal (matching the reference's intent), validates names and respects site-block policies; downsides are some duplicated split logic, empty public policies when no global options are set, and no test for the internal-only case.

Works through forcedAutomatedNames plus a post-internalAP policy built with a refactored split helper and global defaults; all-internal lists rely on the implicit runtime internal fallback, global renewal_window_ratio is not applied, and empty public policies remain possible.

Cleanly extracts the public/internal split helper, adds names via forcedAutomatedNames, and skips names already covered (including hostless-key hosts); however, internal-only name lists get no explicit internal issuer and it skips the global renewal_window_ratio parity.

Sound approach: it reuses a factored-out split helper, applies the global renewal_window_ratio like a site block, dedupes names and keeps http-only names in the automate loader; however, an all-internal name list gets no explicit internal issuer, and an empty public policy can be emitted (subject ordering also differs from the reference).

Similar to C2 with a reusable split helper and renewal_window_ratio parity, plus a valuable Go test checking policy parity with the dummy site block, but internal-only name lists still end up with no explicit internal issuer and it adds noisy empty policies.

The synthetic server block gives exact site-block semantics (renewal ratio, splits, global issuers), and tests are thorough, but wrapping the whole ~200-line pairings loop body in a closure is heavy churn for a small feature, and all-internal names still get no explicit internal policy.

Running the names through a synthetic server block is a neat way to get site-block parity, and names are always listed, but it wraps ~200 lines of the site-block loop in a closure (huge reindentation diff) and still gives a list of only internal names (e.g. just `localhost`) no explicit internal issuer, relying on runtime defaults.

Same segment-indexed pinning approach with a clean hasWBLExpiry helper; it also records mmap-marker refs before the skip (slightly more conservative), and its test checks checkpoint content, restart survival and release after OOO compaction, but does not verify the record is later dropped (the package suite failure is unexplained).

Correctly records duplicate refs per WBL segment, keeps them in checkpoints and releases them after WBL truncation, with a thorough integration test plus a unit case; it locks once per sample during replay, and the repeated t.Cleanup closes of the same db variable are fragile.

Correct fix with the same per-segment tracking (getWBLExpiry returns an unused segment value; mmap-marker remap is moved before the skip); the test leaves background compactions enabled, reads wblExpiries without the lock, and checks the keep function rather than actual checkpoint contents (the package suite failure is unexplained).

Equivalent per-segment pinning with release on truncateOOO, and pinning moved before the mmap-marker skip as a harmless, conservative change; its test does not disable background compactions and reads wblExpiries without the lock.

Correct pin/release logic factored into tidy helpers (hasWBLExpiry, truncateWBLExpiries); the end-to-end test covers restart before and after OOO compaction and the release, but never inspects checkpoint contents and adds no unit case to TestHead_KeepSeriesInWALCheckpoint (the package suite failure is unexplained).

Cleanest variant: small helpers, and pinning placed exactly where the reference puts it; the end-to-end test covers the checkpoint, restart, OOO compaction and a later restart, but it never inspects checkpoint contents directly.

Fixes the root cause by pinning multiRef-resolved WBL refs per segment, keeping their series records in checkpoints and releasing them after WBL truncation, which in practice matches the reference; the end-to-end test checks the record is kept, survives restart and is dropped after OOO compaction, but it takes the mutex per sample during replay and inlines the lock in the closure (the package suite failure is unexplained).

Same sound approach with slightly clunkier inline locking in the keep closure; the strongest test asserts the record is kept in the checkpoint before OOO compaction and dropped from a later checkpoint after it.

Without lastMmapRef it cannot discard chunks cut during replay, so an empty duplicate keeps obsolete data (breaking the existing cleanup), and the maxTime>=minTime filter drops live OOO chunks whose times precede the duplicate's in-order chunks; it fails the hidden test, and its own test only uses a sample-less duplicate record.

Without lastMmapRef it relies on ref and time heuristics. Filtering by the earliest incoming in-order time also drops still-needed OOO chunks, and an empty duplicate leaves chunks created during replay attached. It fails the hidden test and the suite.

Fixes the OOO loss in the hidden scenario, but a duplicate record without chunks leaves replay-created chunks attached because there is no lastMmapRef, which regresses the intended cleanup (package suite fails); it also uses a time cutoff that mixes OOO minTime and rewrites an existing test.

Merges duplicate-ref chunks using time and ref cutoffs, which passes the hidden test. Without lastMmapRef, an empty duplicate leaves compacted chunks created during replay attached, and overlap resolution prefers higher (replay-created) refs. It also rewrites an existing test, and the package suite fails.

Uses lastMmapRef and a replace/keep/merge mode tracker, which is heavier machinery than needed; it appends OOO chunks without sorting by ref (truncation relies on that order), changes the overlap preference to keep the earlier-starting chunk, and the package suite fails despite extensive tests.

Tracks which WAL refs are attached to each live series and switches between replace, keep and merge modes, dropping chunks created during replay; this fixes the reported scenario but is heavy machinery. It appends OOO chunks without sorting by ref, leaves gc's first-chunk assumption unchanged, and the package suite fails.

Threads lastMmapRef like the reference to drop replay-created chunks; the in-order merge (mmc plus later on-disk chunks) keeps time and disk order aligned without the gc change, OOO chunks are unioned, deduplicated and sorted by ref, metrics are tracked accurately, and a multi-restart, all-sample-type test covers the issue scenario.

Passes lastMmapRef and merges instead of replacing. Empty incoming lists keep the existing disk chunks and discard chunks created during replay. In-order chunks become the incoming list plus later existing chunks, and OOO chunks are a deduplicated union sorted by ref. It passes all tests with a solid multi-restart, multi-sample-type test, though the in-order merge is less general than the reference and gc is not hardened.
